title: Stop prompting AI, start onboarding it · hancrafted
description: Why AI underdelivers when you prompt it like a tool, and why onboarding it like a capable new colleague takes management skills, not execution skills: context, tools, a clear brief and checking the work.

The promise and the gap No speaker notes for this Slide.

Twenty times on paper Measured gains are real but uneven Three field experiments with 4,867 developers found a 26% increase in completed tasks for those given a coding assistant, far below “20x”, and each single experiment was noisy. 1 Sources (1) The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers ( opens in a new tab ) papers.ssrn.com People misjudge their own gain In a trial with 16 experienced developers, they forecast a 24% speedup and afterwards believed AI had saved them 20%, while measured time rose 19%. METR marks that result out of date and says it does not show AI fails to speed up most developers, so the point is how unreliable self-perception is, not that AI slows people down. 1 2 Sources (2) Becker, Rush, Barnes, Rein, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org METR, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity (study announcement with limitations) ( opens in a new tab ) metr.org Population-level effects are small so far Linking surveys of 25,000 Danish workers to administrative records found precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT’s launch. 1 Sources (1) Humlum, Vestergaard, Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects (NBER Working Paper 33777) ( opens in a new tab ) nber.org
Day one with a capable stranger No speaker notes for this Slide.

A colleague who knows the written world Vendors brief it as a capable newcomer Anthropic’s prompting guidance says to think of the model as “a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows”, and to test a prompt by showing it to a colleague with minimal context. 1 Sources (1) Anthropic, Be clear and direct (prompting guidance) ( opens in a new tab ) docs.claude.com The lens has a lineage Ethan Mollick first called AI an intern, then in November 2024 dropped “intern” as too constraining and proposed an “infinitely patient new coworker who forgets everything you tell them each new conversation”. 1 Sources (1) Ethan Mollick, Getting started with AI: Good enough prompting, One Useful Thing (24 Nov 2024) ( opens in a new tab ) oneusefulthing.org Developers use the same picture Matt Pocock frames the agent as a colleague “who wakes up every morning and cannot remember who they are”, and says the codebase must be optimized for new starters because an agent starts afresh every session. This rests on the podcast’s published notes, not the full audio. 1 Sources (1) Gergely Orosz, AI Skills with Matt Pocock, The Pragmatic Engineer (17 Sep 2026; podcast notes quoting Pocock) ( opens in a new tab ) newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com

The plan is due by end of day Onboarding as the yardstick Andrej Karpathy framed the real capability test not as solving PhD-grade problems but as whether you would hire it as a junior intern: “get your slack set up, read these onboarding docs, do this task and let’s check in next week”. 1 Sources (1) Andrej Karpathy, post on X (14 Dec 2024) ( opens in a new tab ) x.com

What would you tell them first Write for the newcomer Michael Nygard wrote decision records “as if it is a conversation with a future developer”, so a newcomer need not blindly accept or blindly change a decision. Carried from an earlier research file, not re-fetched. 1 Sources (1) Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions ( opens in a new tab ) cognitect.com Checking is part of the frame Anthropic’s best-practices page says to “Give Claude a way to verify its work” and “If you can’t verify it, don’t ship it”. Carried from an earlier research file, not re-fetched. 1 Sources (1) Anthropic, Claude Code best practices ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com
You managed it, you did not do it No speaker notes for this Slide.

You managed the task A management reading, not a tool reading Harvard Business School’s Joseph Fuller argues companies miss AI’s value because they have not changed how work is organized around it, and that agentic AI is “primarily about managing work”. Only HBR’s summary was read. 1 Sources (1) Joseph Fuller, Create an Onboarding Plan for AI Agents, Harvard Business Review (25 Mar 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) hbr.org The task, not the rank, asks for it The novice boost was measured on bounded tasks inside the model’s competence: 34% more issues resolved per hour for novice support agents against minimal effect for experienced ones. 1 On a task built to lie outside the frontier, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct. 2 That the task demands management discipline, merely correlating with experience, is this Episode’s inference; no source tests it directly. Sources (2) Brynjolfsson, Li, Raymond, Generative AI at Work (NBER Working Paper 31161) ( opens in a new tab ) nber.org Dell’Acqua, McFowland, Mollick, Lifshitz-Assaf, Kellogg, Rajendran, Krayer, Candelon, Lakhani, Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier ( opens in a new tab ) mitsloan.mit.edu Experience with the tool predicts results In Anthropic’s usage data, users with six months or more of tenure show a success rate 3 to 5 points higher within the same task cluster, delegate less by directive and iterate more. Success is Claude’s own assessment and self-selection is not ruled out. 1 Sources (1) Anthropic, Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning Curves (March 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Where the analogy stops A human newcomer learns on the job, an agent does not: Anthropic describes each new session as an engineer arriving “with no memory of what happened on the previous shift”, so anything unwritten is gone. 1 Sources (1) Anthropic Engineering, Effective harnesses for long-running agents (published 26 Nov 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Prompting like a tool, briefing like a colleague Unstated requirements are guessed Models infer a missing requirement correctly only about 41% of the time, and underspecified prompts are twice as likely to regress when the model or prompt changes. 1 Sources (1) Yang, Shi, Ma, Liu, Kästner, Wu, What Prompts Don’t Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Say it up front Across more than 200,000 simulated conversations, every tested model did worse when a task arrived underspecified over several turns than when fully specified at once, by 39% on average. 1 Sources (1) Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville, LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Relevant, specific context, not volume Handing a model the one relevant document lifted question-answering accuracy for GPT-3.5-Turbo from 56.1% to 88.3%, a 2023 retrieval result whose direction transfers and whose size does not. With 20 or 30 documents it could fall below having none. 1 Anthropic: “minimal does not necessarily mean short”. 2 Measured evidence for a human-written brief in non-coding knowledge work is thin. Sources (2) Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, TACL 2024, Table 1 and section 2.3 ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Confident is not correct Invented sources, defended In a New York federal case, lawyers filed a brief citing six cases ChatGPT had invented, defended them when challenged and were fined; the court held that the rules “impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of their filings”. 1 Sources (1) Judge P. Kevin Castel, Mata v. Avianca, Inc., Opinion and Order, No. 22-cv-1461 (PKC) (S.D.N.Y. June 22, 2023), ECF 54 ( opens in a new tab ) storage.courtlistener.com Wrong answers read as coherent On the BCG task outside the model’s frontier, AI users’ wrong answers read as coherent, which made errors harder to catch. 1 Sources (1) Dell’Acqua, McFowland, Mollick, Lifshitz-Assaf, Kellogg, Rajendran, Krayer, Candelon, Lakhani, Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier ( opens in a new tab ) mitsloan.mit.edu A check can be cheap A 19-item surgical checklist was associated with inpatient death falling from 1.5% to 0.8% across eight hospitals. A before-and-after study, and not AI evidence; it shows a simple check can work. 1 Sources (1) Haynes et al., A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population, New England Journal of Medicine 360(5), 2009 ( opens in a new tab ) pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
It feels like a lot No speaker notes for this Slide.

The twist AI as a second pair of eyes Anthropic recommends a second opinion in a fresh context, "so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it". The grill-me link is this Episode's own framing. 1 Sources (1) Anthropic, Claude Code best practices ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com

The promise and the gap 0:00 – 0:15 Open on the hype twenty times every feed keynote vendor deck You have seen the line. Become twenty times more productive with AI. It is on every feed, in every keynote, in every vendor deck. Maybe you even believed it for a day or two. 0:15 – 0:25 Bridge to the room tried it yourself why today Then you sat down and tried it yourself, and you know how that went. So why? Today I want to look at exactly that.

Twenty times on paper 0:00 – 0:13 The number twenty times the promise a whole team Twenty times. That is the promise. Not twenty percent, twenty times. One person doing the work of a whole team. Let us take that at face value, just for a moment. 0:13 – 0:27 Your number your last attempt something real be honest Now think of your own last serious attempt. Something real, not a toy. You got something usable back, maybe even useful. But transformative? Be honest. Not twenty times. Not even close. 0:27 – 0:42 Why, left open the gap Tuesday afternoon hold on to it So there is a gap between the promise and your Tuesday afternoon. Why does it exist? I am going to leave that question hanging. Hold on to it, because I will come back to it.

Day one with a capable stranger 0:00 – 0:14 Switch to the room forget AI Monday morning new colleague coffee in hand Forget AI for a moment. Imagine it is Monday morning, and a new colleague starts today. Take a second and picture them standing at your desk, coffee in hand, ready to go. 0:14 – 0:29 A real task real task real deadline who this person is And you have a real task for them. Not a lecture, not a case study. A real one, with a real deadline. Let me tell you who this person is, and what you need from them.

A colleague who knows the written world 0:00 – 0:15 Profile read everything knowledgeable completely confident never hesitate Here is what you know about them. They have read essentially everything that was ever written down. Extremely knowledgeable, about almost any topic you can name. And they are completely confident. They never hesitate. 0:15 – 0:33 Eager eager to please yes to anything I don't know nothing about your company They are also eager to please. They will say yes to anything, and they will almost never say, I don't know. And one more thing. They know nothing about your company. Not your people, not your budget, not what you did last year.

The plan is due by end of day 0:00 – 0:12 The task Sommerfest Christmas party a hundred people interns to management Here is the task. The company wants a Sommerfest, or a Christmas party, whichever season you like. About a hundred people. Everyone from the interns to the management. 0:12 – 0:30 The clock first day urgent end of day not tomorrow And it is their first day, and it is urgent. A fully structured plan has to be on the desk by end of day. Your team lead wants it. Maybe the CEO wants it. You cannot say it will be ready tomorrow.

What would you tell them first 0:00 – 0:11 Take a second take a second how would you onboard notice what you do first So take a second. Really. How would you onboard this person? Do not think about the right answer. Just notice what you would do first. 0:11 – 0:32 Walk the morning last year's party the budget how many people what our company is like I guess you would start with the morning. You would walk them through last year's party. What worked, what flopped, what the CEO hated. You would tell them the budget. You would tell them how many people are coming, and what our company is like. Formal, casual, loud, quiet. 0:32 – 0:52 Tools and the ask the keys booking login caterer shared calendar what you expect Then you would give them the keys. The login for the booking system. The number of the caterer you trust. Access to the shared calendar so they stop proposing dates that clash. And you would say what you expect. A plan of what shape, for whom, how long. 0:52 – 1:11 Look at the draft not wait until five first draft over lunch check once more your name on it And you would not wait until five o'clock. You would look at the first draft over lunch. Is this going in the right direction? Then you would check it once more before it goes upstairs. Because it is your name on it too.

You managed it, you did not do it 0:00 – 0:13 Pause on the shift what just happened the experiment is over it has a name Now look at what just happened. The experiment is over. Take a breath, because what you just did has a name, and it is not the name you might expect.

You managed the task 0:00 – 0:18 You did not plan the party never opened a spreadsheet set the stage gave access someone checked You did not plan the party. You never opened a spreadsheet or called a caterer. You set the stage. You handed over what you know, you gave access, you said what you wanted, and you made sure someone checked. That was the work. 0:18 – 0:37 Doing became managing doing became managing the shift not a recipe a lens Doing became managing. That is the shift. Do not read it as a recipe, or as a one to one match with anything. It is a lens. And that shift from doing to managing is exactly what working with AI demands of you.

Prompting like a tool, briefing like a colleague 0:00 – 0:17 Back to the hook the gap the question left hanging one line Plan our Sommerfest Now back to the hook. Remember the gap, and the question I left hanging? Think about the last thing you typed into an AI. It was probably one line. Plan our Sommerfest. You would never brief a person like that. 0:17 – 0:35 The answer to the hanging why prompt it like a tool onboard it like a colleague a management task different skills So here is my answer. AI underdelivers when you prompt it like a tool, and the real job is to onboard it like a colleague. And onboarding is a management task, not an execution one. It needs different skills than typing does.

Confident is not correct 0:00 – 0:17 The profile again knowledgeable confident eager to please polished work that may be wrong Go back to the profile for a second. Knowledgeable, confident, eager to please. That is a wonderful combination, and a dangerous one. It hands you polished work that may be wrong, and it hands it over with a smile. 0:17 – 0:32 You check, as with any new hire spot-check the first drafts where a number came from you are responsible So you check it, exactly as you would with any new hire. Spot-check the first drafts. Ask where a number came from. Because whatever goes to the CEO, you are the one responsible. Not the newcomer.

It feels like a lot 0:00 – 0:13 It feels like a lot four disciplines a day-one note every time the work that moved I know. It sounds like a lot. Four disciplines, a day-one note every single time. I will not pretend it is not work. It is. It is the work that moved.

The twist 0:00 – 0:15 The twist AI can help you onboard AI the context you forgot first morning But here is the twist. AI can help you onboard AI. It can interview you for the context you forgot, and ask the questions a good new colleague would ask on their first morning. 0:15 – 0:28 A first step grill-me your next real task all you need to start If you want a first step, there is a simple one called grill-me, which does exactly that. Try it on your next real task. And that is all you need to start.
